1:
The date in the first line is the hardest thing here, since the king named did not begin to reign until the following year. Calvin dismisses two escapes as frivolous or forced, the one counting the years from the beginning of the reign and the one reckoning from the conquest; his conjecture is that either an earlier king of the name is meant, or the son's reign is dated while his father still lived. Ellicott splits the question in two and answers the second in the negative: the verse does not say the city was taken that year at all, since the verb means went rather than came and is the natural word for a Hebrew writing from Babylon, so what is dated is the setting out. The rest follows from the histories: the victory at the river in the fourth year, and only then the advance on the city. Gill keeps two captivities in view, the first leaving the king on his throne as a tributary, with Daniel and his companions held as hostages.

Henry gives the outcome and stands back from it. The city was soon mastered, the king seized, the throne left occupied on tribute for eight years until a rebellion ruined it; from this first deportation most reckon the seventy years, though the destruction came two decades later. What strikes him is one man's life against an empire's: Daniel was carried off that first year and outlasted the whole seventy, so one prophet saw the rise, reign and ruin of the monarchy within his own time. Such short-lived things are the kingdoms of the earth, he says, and the righteous who watch them take root will see them fall.

Keil and Delitzsch anchor the first clause in the histories, where the same event appears as the king becoming a servant and as his being bound. On the vessels they press the idiom: the phrase rendered part contracts an expression meaning from end to end, so what was found throughout contributed its share and much of the whole was taken — the word by itself never meaning a part. Ellicott reads the phrase as from one point to another and infers that the vessels went not all at once but on separate occasions, which Clarke fills out with three removals across the years. Clarke explains what was left and why: the richest pieces went for the service of the foreign god, the rest stayed because the conqueror meant no alteration of the country's constitution, civil or religious, and merely laid it under tribute.

Calvin will not let the doubled sentence pass as two events: it is one statement made twice in different words, the term house standing in that language for any place, as the temple is called God's house. On whose temple it was the voices sharpen the identification by degrees. Clarke names the tutelary god of the city; Ellicott gives the fuller compound name, traces the deity to an older people, and reports that its second element means one who measures the path of the sun; Wesley notes that such divine names were worked into the names of their kings, and that this expedition is where the captives came from, Daniel among them.

Two of them open with the man rather than the date. Clarke says he was of the royal house, carried off very young, and bred so thoroughly in the law that he kept it in a heathen court while a slave; he adds that the reputation became proverbial in his own lifetime. Keil and Delitzsch begin with the name, which means God is my judge or God is judging rather than judge of God, and which two other men in the older books had borne; on the descent they are more cautious than Clarke, leaving open whether he came of the royal seed or only of a distinguished family.
3:
The officer who takes the order is hard to name and easy to place. Gill reports two derivations, one making the name a man of angry countenance, the other a man excelling in wit; Keil and Delitzsch say no satisfactory explanation has yet been found, and identify the man as chief marshal of the court. On the title all agree: it means overseer of the household but is used more widely for a courtier, so Clarke says it signifies officers about the palace whether the men were literally eunuchs or not.

Why these youths were chosen is where Calvin is sharpest. The king demanded them from the nobility, partly to display himself a conqueror, partly to hold hostages, partly on a calculation: boys nourished in his palace would grow estranged from their own people and useful to him, while their noble parentage would keep the nation quiet for fear of what might befall them. Ellicott adds the tradition connecting the four with the last king of Judah and thinks the context admits it; Wesley sees an older prophecy fulfilled in it.

Their age is disputed. Gill will not have them children, making them fifteen or twenty on the ground that a few years later Daniel held posts of real eminence. Calvin puts them at seven or eight. Ellicott reasons from the system rather than the men: a science as elaborate as the Babylonian would need an early start, and the king's later astonishment at Daniel's precocity suggests he was young. Clarke settles for youths and says the word should be so rendered throughout the book.

The list of qualifications is parsed closely. Keil and Delitzsch take the first term for aptitude rather than attainment, an ability to apply themselves to Chaldean learning. Calvin insists on reading one participle actively, since otherwise the repetition would be cold and valueless, and finds eloquence intended: some understand inwardly what they cannot express, so the text notes both the getting of knowledge and the power to communicate it.

The diet is a snare, and two say so. Gill grants the munificence but sees a bait laid to make the young men love their new condition and forget the old. Calvin goes further: where there is cunning in the world it reigns especially in palaces, and a king dealing with an obstinate people wanted servants who would obey without being driven, so he set out to soften them with luxuries — which means his feeding these exiles from his own table is not to be reckoned a virtuous action. Ellicott takes the king more kindly, crediting him with insight enough to prescribe both subjects and length of course. Clarke turns that length into a complaint against his own age: three years sufficed here for a language and its sciences, where Europe spends seven years at school and as many at university to produce a little Latin, Greek and mathematics, and sends out men entitled rather than qualified to teach.

The renaming closes the passage, read as an act of power. Clarke calls it a mark of dominion, the customary imposition of new names on slaves, and works the etymologies: the man whose name meant God is my judge is made the treasury of Bel, and the man whose name meant the Lord is my helper becomes the servant of another god. Gill gives the motives in ascending order: to make them acceptable, to mark them as naturalised subjects, to make them forget the names their fathers gave, and most of all the God whose name those names carried. Keil and Delitzsch compare two kings of Judah renamed by their overlords, and Wesley calls the whole an act of the king's sovereignty. Ellicott adds the detail that repays attention: in one name two letters appear to have been deliberately swapped, so the bearer should not carry a heathen name exactly as it stood.
8:
The refusal is credited to one man and shared by four. Gill takes the singular verb to mean Daniel first thought of it and moved it to the others; Henry makes the point that carries the chapter, that they changed his name but not his nature, and that he worked at the books as hard as anyone while drawing the line at the table.

Why the table was a line divides them. Clarke gives three grounds — unclean animals, animals not properly killed, and animals offered to the gods first — citing a Greek writer who calls the meats at those royal tables victims. Wesley adds that such fare would gratify the flesh and ill suited the exiles' afflicted condition, and calls the refusal a rare pattern of avoiding the occasions of evil. Calvin raises the objection himself, the sharpest thing here: to the pure all things are pure, nothing of the kind is recorded of Joseph, and Daniel very likely ate freely later, so abstaining now looks superstitious or morose, and if right it should have been kept up. His answer is that the abstinence was a defence against being tampered with rather than a rule about food.

Ellicott, without addressing Calvin, supplies what would settle it. The diet is the plain one Daniel's ancestors kept before entering the land, and the reason it was dropped later stands in the book itself, where at the Persian court an older man changes his rule as age tells. He also lays the story beside Joseph's: each finds favour with a master and then a foreign king, each has his faculties enlarged beyond nature, each is sent abroad to comfort an exiled people.

On that favour three insist on the agency. Henry allows that Daniel deserved it and recommended himself by his temper, but notes that the text says God brought him into favour, since not everyone meets acceptance according to his merits, and what interest we think we have made for ourselves must be acknowledged a gift. Gill puts it flatly: the natural gifts might have ingratiated him, but nothing would have overcome a religious prejudice unless the Lord had worked on the man's heart. Keil and Delitzsch locate it in what the officer did not do, since he neither dismissed the request as impertinent nor treated it as punishable, but respected the conviction behind it and raised only the danger.

The danger is real, the refusal gentle. Gill reads the answer as hesitation rather than denial, the man divided between affection and fear; Calvin praises him for what he kept quiet rather than what he granted, since the request would have been fatal had it reached the king, and adds that he is not to be blamed for fearing a man more than God, having no knowledge of God to go on. Keil and Delitzsch give the grammar its force, the question meaning he must not see it, and the closing phrase to forfeit one's head.

So Daniel goes lower down, and Calvin makes the most of it: after one repulse it would have seemed excusable to stop, and the mark of rooted piety is that a man tries every way and does not treat the road as closed. Who the second officer was is unsettled: Gill takes the word for a personal name meaning one in full splendour, while Keil and Delitzsch note the article before it and make it a title from words for wine and head, an overseer of the drink; Ellicott likewise calls him a cellarman, the man Daniel was on easier terms with. The trial is ten days, which Gill thinks long enough for any ill effect to show and Ellicott takes for a round number; Clarke identifies the pulse as seeds and grain, and insists the result was not the diet's doing but a blessing on a diet chosen for religion's sake.
13:
The ten days end better than anyone expected, and nobody credits the vegetables. Gill notes the healthier colour and solid flesh, not the puffiness of disease. Wesley draws the moral, that plain fare under a blessing often yields more health than costly fare does to those who eat the fat. Ellicott sees God beginning to assert himself among the Babylonians and insists the change came of free grace, not of the king's meat. Calvin turns it into doctrine: there is no necessary virtue in bread, which has no life in it and cannot give what it lacks, so what sustains us is a secret blessing; God has determined that our bodies be fed by food and has breathed the power into it, but the life is his and not the loaf's.

The steward comes off less well. Gill observes what became of the rejected portions: the man took them home, and four young gentlemen's rations from the royal table over three years made a handsome addition to his income, so that in serving the Lord's people he served himself. Calvin makes the same observation carry an argument. A man will not pursue a gain that costs him trouble or risk, but let the profit be near and the danger gone and he pursues it naturally; so the permission came only once it could be given safely, and the kindness is not to be credited to the man but to the providence that made him tractable.

On the learning that follows, the question is whose gift it was and of what kind. Henry allows that they were sober and diligent and that their tutors took pains, but ascribes the achievement to God only, and reads it as a balance for what captivity had cost them and a recompence for their integrity. Calvin denies the second half directly: it would be wrong to call the gift a reward for living frugally, since God had another intention, to establish Daniel's authority so that he might afterwards show whose God was the only God. Gill rules out the wrong kind of knowledge, since men who scrupled at the king's table would not have studied the magic and judicial astrology the Chaldeans were addicted to, and God would not have blessed it if they had. Ellicott divides the two terms, giving secular literature to the first, and philosophy, theology and perhaps the reading of portents to the second.

Clarke adds a test for the dreams. Ordinary dreams signify only as much as they cohere, being products of the body, the mind or the day's circumstances; one may be reckoned supernatural when nothing in it is preposterous or monstrous and the order holds from beginning to end.

At the examination the king comes off better than his court. Keil and Delitzsch have the four brought in at the end of the three years, found more intelligent than all the others educated with them, and beyond that superior to every wise man in the kingdom. Gill infers from the questioning that the king was himself a man of learning and judgment, and Wesley agrees, asking how else he could have discerned their fitness, and adding that God was pouring contempt on the pride of the Chaldeans and putting honour on the low estate of his own people. On the last verse three of them guard against a misreading. Ellicott says the word means Daniel lived until that year, not that he prophesied only until then nor that he died in it, the year being named as that of the deliverance; Keil and Delitzsch make the preposition mark a terminus without any claim about what came after; Calvin, noting that a vision is dated two years later, takes the sense to be that Daniel flourished and was acknowledged a prophet through the whole Babylonian period, to the night the last king was killed.
